cim: Last Word: How Artificial Intelligence Is Making Arkansas Business Internationally Competitive
cim_eredeti: Last Word: How Artificial Intelligence Is Making Arkansas Business Internationally Competitive
szoveg_eredeti:
Tucked into a wooded area just off Interstate 530 in Little Rock, GC Evans has quietly built automated packaging solutions for the food and beverage industry since the 1950s. What began as a manufacturer of industrial “coolers and warmers” has evolved into a multiservice company designing and building sophisticated custom systems for packaging operations across the country.

Now one of the technologies reshaping both what GC Evans builds and how the company operates is artificial intelligence.

“With AI, GC Evans can offer the same resources and capabilities that previously only very large companies could offer,” said Mark McNamer, president. “What a staff of 10 could do can now be done more efficiently by just one or two engineers.”

For a relatively small Arkansas manufacturer competing in an increasingly global marketplace, that added efficiency can be significant. AI-assisted tools allow GC Evans engineers to create three-dimensional floor plans and visualize custom packaging solutions with considerably less time and effort. Tasks that once required hours of coding can increasingly be accomplished through simple prompts. Manuals, instructions and technical documentation can be generated in a fraction of the time.

The result is a smaller company capable of offering services, speed and pricing that can compete with much larger international manufacturers.

“Many food and beverage companies would very much like to work with USA-based manufacturers,” McNamer said, “but overseas conglomerates have acquired many of the companies providing automated packaging solutions. AI is one tool we use to even the playing field and bring manufacturing here to Arkansas.”

Artificial intelligence is also becoming part of the machinery itself. For one example, GC Evans manufactures inspection and rejection systems capable of identifying flaws in packaging as products move through a production line. Increasingly, those systems can incorporate AI cameras – machine-vision cameras paired with artificial-intelligence software capable of analyzing products and packaging almost instantaneously.

Rather than relying exclusively on traditional programming to tell a camera exactly what to look for, AI-enabled vision systems can be trained to recognize acceptable products and identify defects or inconsistencies. On a beverage line, that might include damaged cans, improper labels, faulty closures or other packaging problems.

“The AI cameras enable our systems to process 2,000 12-ounce standard aluminum cans per minute,” McNamer said, “and you don’t have to tediously code these cameras. You program the parameters through prompting, which means you don’t need to be a computer scientist to make an adjustment.”

That combination of speed and accessibility illustrates why AI could prove especially consequential for smaller manufacturers. It is not simply automating individual tasks; it is giving smaller teams access to capabilities that once required significantly more personnel, specialized expertise and capital. While much of the national conversation has focused on the possibility that automation will eliminate jobs, McNamer believes the effect could look very different for small and midsize companies.

“While very large companies will likely reduce workforce, smaller companies like GC Evans will increase hiring due to added productivity,” McNamer said. “What we’re looking at is just a shift of workforce to where it is most needed. Like any technology, we will not only adapt to it, but we will also be better for it.”

For Arkansas manufacturers, that may ultimately be one of AI’s greatest opportunities. The technology can give smaller companies the productivity, engineering capabilities and sophisticated tools once available primarily to multinational corporations, allowing Arkansas businesses not simply to compete globally but to bring more of that work home.

Jeremy Harper is the chief instigator for Storm the Castle Creative in Little Rock and director of communications for the Arkansas Research Alliance.
